caveats: This preliminary analysis has not yet been validated in the field and is appropriate for general planning of debris operational responses and related humanitarian action.
name: building-debris-assessment-venezuela-earthquake-june-2026
notes:
This initial quantification of the June 2026 earthquake-induced debris across the most-affected Venezuelan states was derived through a multi-sensor synthetic aperture radar (SAR) change-detection analysis, integrated with rapid building damage assessments and supplemented by visual verification against very high-resolution optical imagery where available. Building footprints, including a modeled height attribute, were sourced from the Global Building Atlas [1] as the baseline layer, with locality-specific damage assessments and an independent SAR-derived damage product incorporated for areas where they were available, as detailed below.

Damage to buildings was assessed through multiple sources and methods. A pixel-wise temporal t-test (PWTT) [2], adapted to a z-score formulation to accommodate the limited number of post-event Sentinel-1 acquisitions available at the time of analysis, was applied to Sentinel-1 Ground Range Detected (GRD) imagery, with buildings scoring above 0.4 retained for further assessment. This was complemented by damage assessment products from Copernicus EMS activation EMSR884 [3], as available on 27 June 2026, and by visual verification using PlanetScope imagery released through Planet's Crisis Response Program [4]. Building damage assessments produced by Microsoft's AI for Good Lab [5], generated by applying a classification model to post-event optical imagery acquired on 25 June 2026, were incorporated in their entirety for Catia La Mar, La Guaira, and Caraballeda. For locations with neither a locality-specific damage assessment nor high-resolution optical coverage, a Sentinel-1 SAR-based damage proxy map distributed via NASA's Disasters Program [6] was incorporated.

This assessment estimates 96,046 buildings to have been damaged or destroyed., corresponding to nearly 3% of all buildings in the assessed states.

For modeling purposes, minimum building height and average story height were considered to be 3m. Each built sq. meter is considered to have generated 1 tonne of debris. For visualization and modelling purposes, results were aggregated into a 7.8 sq. km hexagon grid.  A substantial proportion of the debris remains within structurally compromised buildings and will only become accessible following demolition.

[1] Zhu, X.X., Chen, S., Zhang, F., Shi, Y., & Wang, Y. (2025). GlobalBuildingAtlas: An Open Global and Complete Dataset of Building Polygons, Heights and LoD1 3D Models [Data set]. Technical University of Munich. 
[2] Ballinger, O. (2025). Open access battle damage detection via Pixel-Wise T-Test on Sentinel-1 imagery. Remote Sensing of Environment, 331, 115025.
[3]Copernicus Emergency Management Service (© 2026 European Union), [EMSR884] Earthquake in Venezuela: Damage Assessment Products. Accessed 27 June 2026. 
[4] Planet Labs PBC. (2026). Planet Crisis Response: Venezuela Earthquake, June 2026 [Data set]. Source Cooperative. 
[5] Microsoft AI for Good Lab. (2026). Venezuela Earthquakes: Building Damage Assessment in Catia La Mar, La Guaira, and Caraballeda [Data sets]. Humanitarian Data Exchange (HDX). 
[6] Scher, C., & Van Den Hoek, J. (2026). Damage analysis of Copernicus Sentinel-1 data, Oregon State University [Data set]. NASA Disasters Program, Earthdata GIS.

organization.description: The United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP) and United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) Joint Environment Unit (JEU) responds to environmental dimensions of emergencies by coordinating international efforts and mobilizing partners to support countries that have requested assistance. In doing so, the JEU offers a wide range of services to holistically address the links between environment and emergencies.
